Same $900,000 condo, $13,860 more in tax for the buyer with a mortgage

A $720,000 mortgage brings a gross recording charge of $13,860 at closing. A buyer paying cash for the same condo avoids that charge.

By Pablo Loschi9 October 2026Updated 22 October 20265 min readSources & methods

Two people buy the same $900,000 condo. One pays cash. The other puts 20% down and borrows $720,000. When that loan is recorded at closing, the second buyer owes $13,860 in mortgage recording tax before any credits, on top of the down payment. The cash buyer owes none of it.

The difference comes only from how the home is paid for. It applies below the $1 million mansion-tax line too, and it falls due at the moment a borrower has the least cash to spare.

What this means for a buyer

If you are buying a house or condo with a mortgage, allow for a separate recording-tax calculation on the loan. Credits, exemptions and consolidation arrangements can change the amount. A co-op share loan falls outside this illustration.

A charge on the loan

The mortgage recording tax combines New York State and City levies. The City’s guidance explains the recording requirement and directs readers to ACRIS for a calculation. The tax concerns recording a mortgage against real property. Financing secured by shares in an individual co-op apartment falls outside it.

For the residential loans studied in the paper, the standard borrower schedule is 1.80% below $500,000 and 1.925% at or above that loan amount. Those percentages apply to the mortgage principal. The $900,000 condo example uses the higher rate on a $720,000 loan.

The illustration applies the gross schedule to the entire recorded loan. Actual liability can differ: credits or exemptions may apply, and a consolidation, extension and modification agreement, often called a CEMA, can change the taxable amount. The paper’s calculation does not apply those adjustments.

What the recorded loans add up to

My study links sales and recorded mortgages in Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens from 2016 to 2025. On 174,732 purchases with observed loan amounts, applying the standard borrower schedule gives a gross charge averaging 1.41% of the purchase price for houses and 1.28% for condos. A separate calculation for financed purchases between $300,000 and $6 million, including imputed loans where an amount is missing, puts the gross charge at about $248 million a year.

These are gross charges on each recorded loan, before credits, exemptions and consolidation agreements. A buyer’s actual bill can be lower.

Is the distinction fair?

Paying cash skips the tax. Borrowing triggers it, and the less someone has saved, the bigger the loan and the bigger the tax. A co-op buyer who borrows pays none of it either, because a co-op loan is secured by shares, not by real property. Should needing a loan raise the tax on buying a home?

In May 2026, Albany considered a 1% tax on all-cash purchases of homes above $1 million. The city comptroller reported in June that the proposal was left out of the enacted state budget. The recording tax already distinguishes between buying with cash and borrowing, including below $1 million.

The paper costs an alternative on the same transactions. A charge of about 0.87% of the price on all house and condo purchases in that sample would match the $248 million gross benchmark. Across the replacement schedules tested, about nine in ten financed purchases would have a lower calculated charge. The average reduction for financed purchases is roughly $5,000; purchases without a mortgage match face an average increase of about $11,000 to $13,000. These are fixed-sample calculations before credits and exemptions, not forecasts of revenue or buyers’ responses. A missing mortgage match also does not establish that a buyer paid cash.

The records show the statutory charge but not how much of it ends up with buyers, sellers or lenders.

The same paper examines a different feature of New York’s tax system: the sudden buyer-tax step at $2 million. That story has an interactive illustration of the 2019 thresholds. Mortgage recording charges are excluded from that tool.
